Despite the substantial progress, there remains a knowledge gap between NI and AI, with many complex tasks and areas still unsolved or underdeveloped.  This paper proposes a novel framework, focusing on the fundamental differences and similarities between NI and AI, with an aim to explore the underlying principles and potential boundaries. By exploring these principles, we can harness the significant potential of AI to address some of the world's most pressing issues, while minimizing the risk of unintended consequences. In a particle collision, the Weyl anomaly does not directly affect energy conservation and momentum conservation due to the trace identity for the stress-energy tensor.  However, it may influence conservation laws in processes that produce or absorb a Weyl anomaly-free state with non-zero energy, as the Weyl anomaly then becomes relevant.  We also investigate the effect of Weyl anomaly on the conservation of energy and momentum in a process that produces a Weyl anomaly-free massless fermion state, and derive the modified conservation laws by incorporating the Weyl anomaly through the trace identity.  Furthermore, we analyze the case of a process that produces two massless fermion states of different species, and discuss the possible applications of the modified conservation laws in theoretical high energy particle physics.  We further derive and apply the modified conservation laws to a specific process that produces a Weyl anomaly-free massless fermion state and a real or virtual graviton, and explore its potential implications on the effective description of graviton behavior in high energy particle physics. A time-slotted protocol is employed, and due to the half-duplex constraint, data transmission and reception occur in separate time slots.  As the network aims to achieve exact, confidential data exchange with pairwise nodes while concealing the messages from the remaining N-2 nodes, we establish an optimal strategy for each pair of nodes.  Following this approach, each node will only act as a transmitter or a receiver once throughout the entire process.  As the total number of time slots required is limited to 2N - 2, we demonstrate that exact, confidential data exchange is always possible.  Furthermore, we calculate the minimum number of time slots necessary for each pair to obtain their corresponding messages.  By doing so, we derive a general formula to determine the slot number for each message pair (i, j) as O(log min d_ij, N/d_ij), where d_ij represents the geographical distance between the i-th and j-th nodes.  Moreover, we analyze the network's security by determining the number of time slots that pass before a node becomes aware of more than one message.  Finally, we conclude that the scheme offers ideal security as no node will be aware of more than one message after the process is complete.  As this protocol utilizes an efficient strategy to achieve confidential data exchange, it is highly suitable for sensor networks that prioritize data privacy.  Additionally, due to the lack of repeated time slots, the protocol does not introduce additional communication costs.  As a result, this approach is particularly advantageous for energy-constrained wireless sensor networks. The presence of symmetry in tensor data often significantly affects its structural and computational properties, and thus, the way it is perceived and analyzed.  This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the key concepts related to symmetric tensors, focusing on multilinear representations, particularly in the context of higher-order tensors.  We explore symbolic methods, algebraic geometric techniques, and computational approaches to analyzing and recognizing patterns in symmetric tensor data, along with a discussion of applicable models, including DTensors, STensors, and their variations.  The paper also delves into the theoretical foundations of symmetric tensor decompositions, examining conditions for uniqueness, existence, and rank determination, as well as analyzing algebraic varieties associated with tensor equations.  The paper aims to integrate the distinct aspects of symmetric tensor analysis, highlighting unifying principles, outstanding challenges, and promising research directions.  The paper is written with the intention of serving as a reference guide for researchers and developers in the field of symmetric tensor analysis, as well as providing a foundation for the design of efficient algorithms and theoretical models for analyzing complex network data.  One hour is scheduled for the presentation, allowing for in-depth discussion of the material and opportunities for Q\&A.  The source code for the proposed tutorial is available for download at:  https://github.com/CTADLab/Tutorial-Advances-in-Symmetric-Tensor-Analysis.  The repository includes demo files, code snippets, and additional information to facilitate the tutorial and encourage further exploration of the subject matter.  The proposed tutorial is targeted towards an audience with a strong mathematical background, consisting of researchers and developers in the fields of graph signal processing, machine learning, data science, and computer science.  The tutorial assumes a high level of familiarity with tensor algebra, multilinear representations, and algebraic geometric techniques, as well as a working knowledge of programming languages such as MATLAB and Python.  The tutorial is designed to be highly interactive, with hands-on experience using symbolic computation tools, exploring case studies, and analyzing real-world network data.  The tutorial is organized into five modules, covering the fundamentals of symmetric tensor analysis, DTensors and STensors, algebraic geometric techniques, and applicable models, along with a discussion of open-ended research questions and opportunities for discussion.  The tutorial aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the key concepts related to symmetric tensor analysis, exploring both theoretical and practical aspects, as well as facilitating interaction and feedback from the audience. A key tool in analyzing this relationship is the optical depth, which gauges the probability that a particle's interaction with gravitational waves leads to Hawking radiation and subsequent decay.  Building on previous work, we have calculated the optical depth for massless particles, focusing on the scalar, photon, and graviton cases, and also extended the analysis to include fermions.  A novel finding is that the optical depth growth rate exceeds a critical value for particles with energies above $10^{-10}$eV.  Notably, this rate differs significantly between different types of particles, with electrons, muons, and neutrinos exhibiting the most substantial growth.  To further contextualize these findings, we have also computed the energy spectra of gravitational waves for point sources with various masses, ranging from $10M_{sun}$ to $10^{5}M_{sun}$.  A notable outcome is that, for masses above $10^{21}gram$, even the most optimistic estimates of particle detection probabilities fall below the signal background.  Ultimately, our research suggests that, given current limitations in detection technology, the majority of information contained in gravitational waves is unlikely to be directly observable.  However, as the optical depth is a measure of the probability that a particle's interaction with gravitational waves leads to Hawking radiation, it also marks the beginning of a new pathway of decay that can potentially reveal this information to observers.  As a result, we propose a novel scenario where, despite the minuscule probability, the conversion of gravitational waves into particles could potentially outpace Hawking radiation as the primary information-carrying mechanism for black holes.  This novel perspective offers a compelling alternative to the information paradox, reconciling quantum mechanics with general relativity by extending the definition of black hole entropy to include the contributions from gravitational waves.  Furthermore, our research finds that this expanded entropy formulation aligns with established theories, including loop quantum gravity and the holographic principle. Given the structure of the model, we derive expressions for the basic reproduction numbers of infected and recovered individuals, demonstrating their direct relationship with the classic expression for the basic reproduction number in traditional compartmental models.  Notably, we establish conditions under which the model's epidemic peak occurs before the population cohort with the highest infection risk has reached maximum size, a critical factor in shaping the course of an epidemic.  To analyze the model's behavior dynamically, we compute the characteristic equations for the linearized epidemic system, analyzing the conditions under which multiple positive eigenvalues emerge, signaling a growth surge in cases of a specific age group.  In response to changing epidemic conditions, we observe that the model's epidemic peak adapts proactively, ensuring that the population cohort with the highest infection risk experiences the most significant surge in cases.  To validate these findings, we develop a simulation framework, demonstrating the model's capability to replicate realistic epidemic patterns in response to various infection scenarios.  Ultimately, our research highlights the significance of accurately modeling Age-specific rates of infection and recovery in epidemic modeling, allowing for a more nuanced understanding of epidemic behavior and the development of targeted public health strategies.  Additionally, our approach provides a versatile framework for analyzing epidemic models categorized by demographic characteristics, paving the way for future applications in various epidemic scenarios.  To facilitate widespread utilization, we make our code available online at https://github.com/jacobchekof/ARModel.  Furthermore, we contribute a comprehensive mathematical foundation for analyzing multi-group epidemic models on the network N, accessible via the arXiv preprint at http://arXiv.org/abs/math.BA/2106.14631.  This research has implications for various epidemic scenarios, including the COVID-19 pandemic, enabling health officials to prioritize high-risk populations in response to evolving epidemic conditions and optimizing limited resources in the face of uncertain infection data.  In areas with reliable data availability, health authorities can directly apply our results, targeting the population cohort with the highest infection risk most aggressively with intervention measures.  In regions with scarce data availability, our approach offers a scientifically grounded framework for prioritizing high-risk populations, enabling health officials to make data-driven decisions based on theoretical models, as validated through simulation experiments. involving multiple energy sources and large storage capabilities is a complex task.  As the system's energy sources and storage capabilities can change over time, a dynamic approach to generating and storing energy is necessary to meet changing demand and generate a steady state of the system.  A control strategy that balances the system's generation and storage in real-time is crucial to achieve a stable power output.  In this study, we present a decentralized method for managing a large-scale power system that consists of various energy sources and large storage capabilities.  A network of generators and storage units is controlled to produce a stable power output by adjusting their production and release in real-time based on changing energy demands.  The system's stability is ensured by implementing a consensus mechanism among the units, which allows them to communicate with each other and agree on the optimal production and release of energy.  A group of leaders is also chosen from the storage units to determine the overall production and release of energy that is necessary to meet changing demands.  A mathematical model is developed to analyze the system's stability and convergence, and it is shown that the control strategy leads to a stable power output that converges to the desired state within a finite time.  A real-world example is also provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of the control approach.  In this example, ten units of generators and ten units of storage devices are used to produce a power output that meets changing demands of 1000MW.  The results show that the system's power output converges to the desired state within 20 seconds.  The control approach is also shown to outperform an existing method that uses a central leader, which is a limitation in real-world applications due to communication delays and the possibility of leader unit failure.  The proposed control strategy is suitable for large-scale power systems that consist of various energy sources and large storage capabilities, and it has the potential to be applied in other complex network systems.  The contributions of this study are twofold.  The first contribution is the development of a decentralized control approach that leads to a stable power output in a large-scale power system with multiple energy sources and large storage capabilities.  The second contribution is the analysis of the system's stability and convergence, which provides valuable insights into the underlying dynamics of the control strategy.  The proposed control approach can be applied in real-world power systems that consist of various energy sources such as solar, wind, and hydro power, and it can be used to produce a stable power output in systems with large storage capabilities such as pumped hydro storage and battery energy

of 3D structures from images of biological macromolecules.
  While single particles like viruses and proteins can be effectively reconstructed using EM, the process is more complicated for more complex biological systems like cells and tissues that comprise numerous identical particles arranged in a defined lattice.
  Cryo-EM techniques have significantly improved, allowing for the direct reconstruction of 3D structures from EM images of lattice-formatted biological samples.
  By multiplying an individual particle's 3D structure by a lattice of known dimensions, it's possible to obtain a high-resolution 3D model of a biological sample's native conformation and/or binding sites. 
  This direct approach to 3D reconstruction bypasses the single-particle method, reducing data processing needs and overcoming limitations associated with particle recognition and classification. 
  This technique has successfully yielded high-resolution structures for various samples, including bacteria, viruses, and proteins, and holds promise for further applications. 
  This review discusses the principles, advantages, and challenges of direct 3D reconstruction from lattice-formatted biological samples, as well as the method's potential applications and future directions. 
  This technique is particularly valuable for determining the structures of biological samples that cannot be crystallized or that have large unit cells, and for identifying binding sites for molecules that bind to a sample. 
  It also has the potential to aid in the development of new pharmaceuticals, facilitate a deeper understanding of various biological processes, and contribute to the creation of novel biosensors. 
  This method could also be applied to non-biological materials with defined lattices, enabling researchers to visualize the shapes of nanomaterials and their interfaces with cells and tissues. 
  This review also explores the possibility of using this technique to obtain 3D models of biological samples with partially defined lattices, such as muscle fibers and collagen bundles, and for determining the structures of multiple components within a single non-covalent complex. 
  This approach could potentially be used in conjunction with other methods like small-angle X-ray scattering and cryo-ET to gain a more comprehensive understanding of various biological systems at multiple scales. 
  This review provides a comprehensive overview of the direct 3D reconstruction technique from lattice-formatted biological samples for the EM community and researchers in related fields. 
  This technique has the potential to significantly contribute to our understanding of various biological systems and processes, and could lead to the discovery of novel pharmaceutical targets. 
  This review is designed to be accessible to researchers with limited knowledge of EM and 3D reconstruction

By applying this metric to the matrix algebra A^(m,n), we derive a distinctive variety of ideals whose degree correspondence mirrors the Krull dimension. Despite the development of sophisticated models like PYTHIA and DGLAP, the formation zone at the onset of hadronization remains poorly understood. Furthermore, the current state of knowledge fails to provide a clear definition of the formation zone itself, employing instead a collection of loosely related length scales such as Bethe--Weizs\"acker mass parameters, screening lengths in lattice QCD, and minimal sensitivity regions in transport coefficients. In contrast, we propose a unified picture of the hadron formation mechanism, focusing on the role of quark antiquark pairs in the hadronization process. By examining key features of the Feynman diagram approach, we outline a clear, metric-independent definition of the formation zone.   We derive a generalized dynamics that respects the Markovian framework while capturing non-Markovian behaviors.
  Our approach focuses on the environment's reduced density matrix evolution, emphasizing the role of initial conditions in distinguishing non-Markovian periods.
  Within this generalized dynamics, we identify conditions under which traditional Markovian descriptions apply or fail to apply, highlighting the significance of the environment's correlation time and initial state memory.  Our method provides a foundation for incorporating non-equilibrium effects into open system dynamics, offering a perspective that prioritizes the environment's influence and memory.  As a concrete example, we examine and contrast the Lindblad equation and a non-Lindblad dynamics resulting from localized and delocalized environment configurations, illustrating the significance of initial conditions in distinguishing non-Markovian periods.  In the case of a harmonic oscillator environment, we derive a closed-form expression for the memory kernel, demonstrating how non-Lindblad dynamics arises from a reservoir with properties similar to an optical cavity.  This theoretical framework offers a versatile tool for analyzing and modeling open system behavior in complex environments, providing a platform for exploring various scenarios, including multi-mode processes and environments with spin statistics.  As the approach prioritizes the environment's influence and memory, it is particularly suited for describing open system dynamics in optomechanical systems, cavity QED, and similar scenarios.  Furthermore, our description aligns with recent proposals for using memory effects to address the consistency issue in forward and backward time evolution, allowing for a coherent representation of non-Markovian dynamics throughout the system's history.  By extending the scope of the generalized dynamics to the environment itself, we set the stage for developing a coherent, closed description of open system evolution, enabling the exploration of scenarios where the system and environment exchange influence and memory.  As a proof-of-concept, we outline a strategy for deriving an extended Fokker-Planck approach that incorporates backward time evolution, illustrating the potential for incorporating historical influence and memory into open system descriptions.  This research contributes to a broader theoretical framework for reconciling forward and backward time evolution in open system quantum mechanics, offering a foundation for developing coherent descriptions of influence and memory exchange between systems and environments. yelinating disease of the central nervous system characterized by variable lesion distribution and unpredictable symptom onset. Although current theories attempt to explain the non-random pattern of lesions in MS, none have been extensively tested or proven. Furthermore, the lack of a consensus model hinders the development of effective prediction tools and compensates for the uncertainty in clinical decision-making. In this work, we present a data-driven analysis of lesion distribution in a large cohort of MS patients and propose a novel probabilistic model to describe the process. Our findings indicate that lesion formation in MS is a Poisson process, occurring randomly throughout the central nervous system, except in areas already affected by lesions. As a result, we observe a positive correlation between the volume of existing lesions and the probability of new lesion formation at a given brain location. Our model aligns with current diffusion tensor imaging findings, which show that areas with high axonal damage are less likely to develop new lesions. By applying our model to real-world scenarios, we demonstrate its potential to predict new lesion locations and volume, as well as its utility in designing efficient lesion targeting areas for clinical trials. Our findings provide a foundation for a new understanding of MS lesion formation and offer a practical, universally applicable model for researchers and clinicians to use. We re-examine the X-ray non-detection data and find that it actually supports the shock-breakout model for dust shell eruptions, similar to SN 2004ew.  A key factor is considering the critical role that relativistic particles play in producing X-rays, distinct from their role in radio emission.  The non-detection of X-rays from these events is consistent with their lower energies compared to SN 2004ew, and indicates that even the most massive dust shells might not always be inflated by relativistic jets.  We also propose a new theoretical understanding of giant dust shell eruptions as a distinct category of astrophysical events, driven by massive star interactions with their surrounding medium, rather than supernovae explosions.  This perspective offers exciting possibilities for observing these enigmatic events in the X-ray and gamma-ray spectra.  Ultimately, the analysis contributes to a broader picture of massive star explosions and their impact on their surroundings.  Based on the proposed theory, we predict that future X-ray and gamma-ray observations could discover hundreds of giant dust shell eruptions in nearby galaxy star-forming regions.  This prediction is particularly significant for upcoming and planned missions such as eROSITA, XMM-Newton, and the Gamma-Ray Transient Monitor.  Furthermore, the analysis suggests that giant dust shell eruptions might be associated with some Fast Blue Optical Transients (FBOTs) observed in galaxy star-forming regions.  This connection is particularly notable for FBOT-like events AT2019dqr and AT2017euh.  Finally, the study recommends that the community consider developing new observational criteria for detecting these enigmatic events, as well as the creation of dedicated follow-up programs for identifying giant dust shell eruptions in X-ray and gamma-ray spectra. Specifically, quaternions don't observe the key property that orthogonal transformations preserve norm magnitude. Consequently, a direct application of the Euclidean norm in quaternion space to solve problems such as finding nearest quaternion orthogonal to a given unit quaternion isn't possible. To address this issue, we introduce a new norm that aligns with quaternion geometry by mimicking complex number geometry. By defining a mapping that sends a quaternion and its conjugate to a complex number, we derive a norm that mirrors the complex number Fubini-Study norm. With this new norm at our disposal, we can effectively solve problems related to quaternion orthogonal transformations by leveraging the established connection to complex number geometry. As a concrete example, we present a scenario where the shortest path between two unit quaternions representing 3D rotation movements corresponds to the great circle defined by the new norm. Although both images and point clouds contain spatial information, their unique characteristics necessitate the use of non-uniform grids to process and describe their three-dimensional structure.  Unlike images that are represented by two-dimensional grids, point clouds are described using three-dimensional grids with irregularly spaced points that offer limited information about the presence of objects between data points.  Due to these distinct properties, networks designed for image analysis are not effective for point cloud analysis and vice versa.  To address this challenge, various network architectures have been proposed that tailor the processing of image and point cloud data to its unique characteristics.   We investigate the theoretical foundations of Bayesian model choice and inference in econometrics using data that is partially observed and subject to noise, drawing on Bayesian factors, marginal likelihood and information criteria.
  Our study reveals that the typical objective behind these methods, aiming to identify the true model or its parameters, might be misguided due to the fundamental issue of overfitting in model choice and the bias inherent in Bayesian factor estimates. 
  Furthermore, we find that existing approaches often rely on unverified assumptions and may yield inconsistent results, especially when dealing with underdetermined systems of equations. 
  To address these challenges, we develop novel theoretical analyses, proposing alternative methods that can determine the number of underlying factors in a multiple linear regression model and the number of structural shocks in a vector autoregressive model. 
  Our findings lead to the creation of data-driven Bayesian factor criteria that outperform their conventional counterparts in various simulation scenarios and truly represent the true underlying structure of econometric models. 
  These findings contribute significantly to the Bayesian econometrics literature, offering a comprehensive framework for evaluating and estimating complex econometric models. Using data from Google Trends to estimate the influence of lockdown policies on casual work, this study contradicts the prevailing view that the pandemic significantly reduced informal employment.  In fact, it is found that casual work actually increased in response to lockdowns, with the most significant effects observed in sectors most severely impacted by lockdowns, such as accommodation and food services.  A possible explanation for this counterintuitive finding is that formal jobs became riskier during the pandemic, causing individuals to opt for informal work to minimize their exposure to health risks and job loss.  This research contributes to the growing body of evidence highlighting the resilience of informal employment and underscores the importance of distinguishing between formal and informal employment in economic research.  Furthermore, it suggests that policymakers should consider the potential consequences of lockdown policies on informal employment and consider alternative strategies that directly target high-risk sectors.  Additionally, this study proposes that central banks could play a more active role in mitigating the effects of lockdowns on informal workers by implementing monetary policies that favor sectors with lower informal employment rates.  Ultimately, this study advocates for a more nuanced understanding of labor market responses to lockdown policies and encourages further research on the subject.  The findings presented in this study could also be applied to other crises, such as natural disasters, offering valuable insights for policymakers, economists, and researchers alike.  The data used in this study is available for replication purposes, with the estimates validated using multiple Google Trends datasets from various sources, including Google Keyword Planner and Wikipedia page views. routing problems where vehicles may be unavailable due to factors like broken charging cables or full batteries that cannot be easily replenished on the go.  We have analyzed three variations of the Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP), each with a distinct set of constraints related to vehicle unavailability.  The first variant, which we call the Fixed Unavailable VRP, requires a predetermined number of vehicles to be idle at specific depots to address the issue.  The second variant, the Dynamic Unavailable VRP, allows for an unlimited number of idle vehicles at each depot to address the issue.  We also examined a third variant that combines elements of the first two options.  Our research utilized a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model to solve these problems, and we evaluated three different solvers (CPLEX, Gurobi, and Scip) to determine the most effective one for each variant.  We tested a range of scenarios with randomly generated data to assess the performance of each solver in each variant.  The results showed that Gurobi consistently yielded the best solutions for the Fixed Unavailable VRP, while CPLEX performed the best for the Dynamic Unavailable VRP.  We further analyzed two real-world case studies to evaluate the applicability of these models.  The first case study involved 20 vehicles and 100 customers, and the second case study involved 50 vehicles and 200 customers.  The models demonstrated promising outcomes for both scenarios, with the potential to achieve significant cost savings by optimizing vehicle usage.  The results from the real-world case studies showed that the models could effectively address the issues related to vehicle unavailability and generate efficient routing solutions that minimized driving distances and reduced the number of vehicles required.  The models also proved capable of handling large datasets with an average of 5000 variables and 15000 constraints.  The overall findings suggest that these models can be utilized to address real-world EVRP problems and provide a valuable framework for future research.  The paper contributes to the existing literature on VRP by introducing a novel variation of the problem and exploring the effectiveness of different solvers.  The results offer valuable insights into the applicability of these models for real-world EVRP problems and provide a foundation for further research on the topic.  The models align with industry trends towards the use of electric vehicles and offer a practical solution for companies looking to adopt this technology.  The paper also offers a theoretical contribution by extending the existing literature on VRP and providing a framework for analyzing similar problems in the future.

Since star formation in these galaxies shapes chemical composition, observing metallicity allows us to probe their history of star formation and formation processes.  Analyzing the relationship between galaxy mass and metallicity, we identify a discrepancy between more massive faint dwarfs and less massive ultra-faints, which cannot be explained by theoretical models that account for gas enrichment and ejection of enriched material through supernovae explosions.  However, incorporating stellar feedback into hydrodynamic simulations resolves this gap, demonstrating that more massive dwarfs experience more intense starbursts, leading to faster enrichment and ejection of metal-bearing gas.  Using these simulations, we develop a simple analytical model that quantifies the efficiency of enrichment ejection, allowing us to reconstruct the metal enrichment history of these galaxies.  Applying this model to individual galaxies yields similar results to observed data, demonstrating its effectiveness.  As the most massive galaxies have the highest metallicity, we use the model to determine the minimum mass required for gas to become self-enriching, estimating that ultra-faint dwarfs need at least $10^{6.5}$ times the mass of the Segue 2 galaxy to achieve a metallicity of 1/100th of the solar value.  Finally, we examine the implications of our findings on our understanding of dwarf galaxy evolution, suggesting that more massive faint dwarfs are likely the remnants of smaller more massive precursors that have undergone significant star formation and enrichment, while the least massive ultra-faint dwarfs might be the first stars to form in the universe with minimal enrichment. uncertainty in quantum cryptography using continuous-variable optics comes from the lack of an accurate model for photon detection processes.  As a crucial area of investigation, research has focused on reconciling theoretical descriptions of photon detection with the practical realities of optical experiments.  Despite the importance of this research, there's a noticeable scarcity of experimental data available for testing and validating the theoretical models used in this field.  To bridge this gap, we conducted precise optical measurements of spontaneous parametric down-conversion occurring within a nonlinear beta-barium borate crystal, allowing us to accurately determine the detection efficiency of optical detectors for photons of varying energies.  By doing so, we were able to experimentally validate the commonly employed definition of detector efficiency, which we found to be inaccurate in certain situations.  Furthermore, we derived a new, more nuanced definition of detector efficiency that takes into account the distinct generation mechanisms of signal photons in optical quantum cryptography.  Additionally, we observed a notable discrepancy between the theoretical models of photon detection processes, which prompted a critical examination of existing approaches.  To contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of the subject, we conducted a thorough analysis of the factors influencing the generation of twin photons, exploring various scenarios involving different wavelengths, beam shapes, and angle configurations.  Through this research, we aimed to provide a solid foundation for developing more precise models of photon detection processes, which would have a positive impact on the development of continuous-variable optical quantum cryptography and related fields. A prominent variety, known as SNARKs, offer proof verification that is complex and time-consuming, justified by allowing multiple verifiers to check the same proof, which is a hallmark of their practical utility. However, the current state of technology restricts most SNARKs to a single verifier due to the high computational requirements of verification.  In response, a novel construction called Quorums and SNARKs (QSNARKs) has been proposed, which enables the creation of proofs that can be verified by a quorum of verifiers, meaning a group of verifiers that exceeds a certain threshold.  QSNARKs leverage secret sharing techniques to distribute proof components among verifiers, with the aim of ensuring that a quorum is achieved only when sufficient, properly positioned verifiers are present.  Building upon the QSNARKs framework, we have designed a new scheme called Turbulence QSNARKs, which offers significant improvements over the existing options, with the added benefit of being highly resistant to tampering and manipulation.  Our contribution outperforms the current standards in several key areas, including a dramatic reduction in verification time, an increase in the number of available hash functions, and an expansion of the application scope to more complex network scenarios.  The core idea behind our scheme is attributable to the successful integration of Twist-Reduced ECC (TTRECC) and the Turbulence Winternitz signature scheme, which produces a robust and efficient proof verification process.  The code for our Turbulence QSNARKs is available for public use, offering a promising alternative to the existing SNARK options by providing a viable template for constructing new, quorum-enabled proof systems.  Moreover, our design's modular structure allows for the easy creation of customized QSNARKs suitable for a wide range of use cases and applications, along with already-identified-scenarios such as social networks, blockchain consensus mechanisms, and the management of distributed ledgers, as well as novel scenarios such as verifiable multi-party computations in the presence of adverse actors and the development of fair and trustworthy roulette games.  In addition, our scheme accommodates a variety of pre-existing hash functions, including SHA-2, SHA-3, BlueWallet's custom hash function, and the widely-used cryptographic primitives SM9, NewHope, and RingNewHope, in addition to commonly used cryptographic schemes such as ECDSA, Ed25519, and BLS12-381, ensuring its applicability across diverse network architectures

Previous studies have explored how certain inputs can elicit specific outputs from specific parts of neural networks, but they rarely consider the overall structure of the network in relation to the information it contains.   Recent studies have explored the microstructural evolution of this material following severe high-strain rate deformation, focusing on its crystal structure and magnetic properties.
  This research aims to investigate how the B20-type cobalt germanide responds to severe high-strain rate deformation on a mesoscale, examining how deformation impacts its microstructure and properties.
  Using in situ high-energy X-ray diffraction and magnetic measurements during deformation, we can determine how the material's crystal structure and magnetic properties evolve in real-time.
  Following deformation, we conducted ex situ transmission electron microscopy to analyze the material's nanoscale structure and composition.
  Our findings reveal that the B20-type cobalt germanide undergoes significant twinning and grain refinement following severe high-strain rate deformation.

Given a simple closed curve in three-dimensional Euclidean space, the tube method enables the construction of a minimal surface by rotating a curve defined within a narrow tube about its central axis. This construction yields a minimal surface if the curve's shape is specifically defined, which often happens when the curve is a circle or an ellipse.  This paper explores novel applications of the tube method or the volume-of-tube approach to solve problems involving minimal surfaces, focusing on scenarios where the underlying domain is enclosed by multiple, possibly intersecting circles or curves. However, the effectiveness of these techniques relies on their ability to accurately forecast missing data, which poses a significant risk if they incorporate biases.  Unfortunately, existing studies have demonstrated that popular machine learning algorithms can indeed perpetuate existing disparities within datasets, which is particularly concerning when the data is used to train models that make critical decisions.  To better understand the relationship between data biases and prediction errors, we conducted an in-depth theoretical analysis, which revealed that algorithms preferentially err on minority groups affected by biased data.  Furthermore, we conducted experiments using real-world datasets, which confirmed our findings and demonstrated that the source of bias in the data directly influences the areas where errors occur.  Ultimately, our research provides valuable insights for developers, data scientists, and regulators on the potential consequences of data flaws and the importance of considering data quality standards.  Moreover, our findings offer a foundation for addressing biases in prediction models by providing a clear understanding of how data flaws impact model behavior.  By doing so, we hope to encourage the creation of more equitable data standards and analysis methods.  One promising approach we identified is inverse validation, which we demonstrated to be an effective tool in a real-world dataset scenario.  Lastly, we propose a novel fairness metric called errancy bias, which we believe holds significant potential for improving model performance by prioritizing the most biased errors for correction.  As this approach is particularly suitable for visual data such as images and videos, we also developed a working prototype that successfully eliminated biases in image classification models.  We anticipate that this prototype will serve as a valuable starting point for the development of automated error correction tools. As a result, there is a growing interest in adapting and fine-tuning pre-trained LMs for specific languages that have limited resources.  Despite the impressive capabilities of these models, they often struggle with languages that use non-standard scripts, such as Devanagari, which is the case with several Indian languages.  The scarcity of native language data for these scripts further exacerbates the challenge.  To address this issue, researchers have explored the use of LMs trained on scripts that are more prevalent, which might not be the native script of the language in question.  However, LMs trained on scripts that are more prevalent may not perform effectively with languages that use non-standard scripts, mainly due to differences in script and language characteristics.  A recent study found that LMs trained on scripts that are more prevalent may excel with languages that use similar scripts, but this success is not guaranteed for languages that use non-standard scripts.  To investigate the feasibility of using prevalent script LMs for languages that use non-standard scripts, we conducted experiments with five Indian languages that use the Devanagari script, which are Marathi, Nepali, Rajasthani, Sindhi, and Bhojpuri.  Our results showed that LMs trained on more prevalent scripts do not perform well with languages that use non-standard scripts, demonstrating a significant gap in accuracy.  However, we observed a positive correlation between the frequency of character combinations and LM accuracy, which prompted us to explore an approach that prioritizes training data featuring characteristic combinations.  Our findings revealed that by optimizing the training data, we can enhance LM performance for languages that use non-standard scripts, which is evident in a substantial improvement in accuracy.  Our method outperformed the standard approach in all five languages, achieving significant gains in accuracy across various tasks, which included poetry prediction, sentence prediction, and spell checking.  Our results provide valuable insights into the limitations of prevalent script LMs and the advantages of optimizing training data for languages that use non-standard scripts.  Our approach offers a promising solution to this challenge, which is available for public use, along with the code and data, to facilitate the development of language models for languages that use non-standard scripts.   adaptive filtering to estimate background noise.  This approach offers several
  advantages, including improved prediction accuracy, reduced computational needs,

As existing theoretical models are insufficient to analyze the complexity of neural network functions, we introduce a new framework based on descriptive complexity measures, specifically using choice and least first order logic. (LISA), scheduled to launch in the 2030s, will observe gravitational waves of varying frequencies. Initially, LISA is expected to detect waves with very low signal-to-noise ratios, making precise parameter estimation challenging.  A key issue in analyzing LISA data is the identification of binary systems that produce noticeable effects.  As the most significant impact of a gravitational wave observation is the phase shift it induces, using phase information could aid system identification.  A recently proposed method, involving the use of phase derivatives to identify system characteristics, has shown promise.  Building on this idea, we investigate using phase derivative features in a machine learning framework to classify binary system parameters.  Our research uses simulated signal data to evaluate the effectiveness of phase-based features in distinguishing parameters of compact binary mergers.  We find that, compared to traditional frequency and amplitude features, phase-based features lead to significant improvements in classification accuracy.  Furthermore, we observe that certain phase feature combinations exhibit a direct correlation with fundamental wave properties, making it possible to estimate key parameters of detected waves.  One such combination, involving the first and second phase derivative peaks, has been identified as particularly valuable.  Our results suggest that, in the case of equal mass mergers, this pair of features can be used to estimate individual masses.  Our findings contribute to the development of an efficient, phase-focused approach for identifying binary system characteristics in LISA data, setting the stage for future optimization studies. While incorporating data into automated systems may improve their performance, doing so in a manner that respects fairness towards various subpopulations is crucial, as prejudice can be embedded and exacerbated through biased data.  Although numerous studies have investigated methods to guarantee fairness, most assume a fixed and known distribution of subpopulations, which might not always hold true in practical scenarios.  In contrast, our research focuses on a context where important characteristics defining subgroups are unknown, which is common in many real-world applications.  We introduce a novel concept of fairness, which prioritizes ensuring similar treatment probabilities across subgroups based on a desired categorization of the population, rather than one that is currently known.  Furthermore, we propose an optimization framework that can accurately identify subgroups with disparate treatment needs, which aligns with various objective functions, leaving room for various analysis approaches.  Theoretical justifications demonstrate the proposed approach meets established standards of fairness, while empirical evaluations on simulated and real-world data sets confirm its effectiveness.  By extending traditional fairness measures and providing a practical tool for unsupervised subgroup detection, our research contributes significantly to the field of fair decision-making. The cold dark matter (CDM) model, combined with a linear power spectrum, has been successful in predicting the halo formation process, which then leads to the formation of galaxies.  However, since dark matter is unidentified, its properties cannot be directly determined, leaving uncertainty about how it behaves, particularly regarding its potential and velocity dispersion.  The theory of structure formation is complex, involving both gravitational physics and the properties of the dark matter itself, making assumptions about its behavior crucial.  Over the vast scales involved in halo formation, the influence of the dark matter potential and velocity dispersion is distinct, leading to different formation timescales.  A team of researchers conducted a comprehensive survey of non-relativistic Lattice Field Theory simulations to determine the halo mass dependence of the average halo formation timescale, aiming to link it with the universal halo mass function observed in the universe.  To achieve a precise calculation, the researchers accounted for the distinct impacts of the halo potential and velocity dispersion, utilizing a simplified model that approximated the halo formation process as a one-to-one correspondence with the transfer function of linear density fluctuations.  The results showed a direct relationship between the formation timescale and the peak height of the density fluctuation profile, consistent with earlier findings based on the excursion set model.  The team also derived a simple analytical formula to predict the halo formation timescale, which demonstrated a coefficient of proportionality inversely related to the velocity dispersion of the dark matter, in line with theoretical expectations.  To further analyze the relationship between the formation timescale and the velocity dispersion of the dark matter, the researchers conducted a series of thought experiments, exploring different scenarios of halo growth, including the merger-driven growth of massive halos and the formation of small halo-like structures within existing galaxies.  The results provided valuable insights into the underlying physical processes, suggesting that the formation timescale was more closely tied to the potential depth of the dark matter than its velocity dispersion, which was contrary to the linear fluctuation approximation but consistent with the simplified model used.  The research offered a novel perspective on the formation timescales of galaxy-sized halos, offering a possible explanation for the observed paucity of massive halos in the present-day universe.   Our analysis focuses on the graph theoretical implications of switching patterns, examining how the sequence in which controllers are activated affects system dynamics and stability.
  We introduce a concept called "reducibility" to evaluate switching patterns, assessing how quickly the system's dynamics decay after controller activation.

  We believe our research contributes significantly to our understanding of switching protocols in multi-agent systems, offering promising avenues for further investigation. By directly solving the Euler equations, our method bypasses the need for a prior knowledge of the initial vortex density, and is also not limited to cases with moderate initial vortex stretching.  Furthermore, we have extended the classical method by including an additional source term that aligns with the local flow direction, which is particularly beneficial for describing ring vortex evolution.  To evaluate our method's effectiveness, we compared its output against direct Euler equation solutions and found a high level of agreement.  To further assess its applicability, we applied our approach to various initial condition configurations, which resulted in accurate ring vortex formation, evolution, and eventual decay.  To facilitate practical use, we have made the code available for public access.  As the algorithm is based on the Euler equations, it retains their physical properties, including conservation of momentum, angular momentum, and energy in inviscid cases, and further includes viscosity-induced decay in viscous situations.  To facilitate practical application, we have embedded the algorithm within the framework of a composite initial condition model, which outperformed traditional vortex density-based approaches in various test scenarios.  To validate the model's theoretical stability, we analyzed the development of instabilities in swirling flows and found a positive correlation between ring vortex formation and Kelvin-Helmholtz instability growth.  To further explore the relationship between ring vortex evolution and fluid instability, we conducted simulations of unstable rotating shafts and found a direct link between ring vortex formation and shaft vibration amplitude.  To expand the model's scope, we applied the algorithm to an initial condition mimicking a satellite's debris disk evolution simulation, which resulted in the formation of spiral structure precursors.  To evaluate the model's capability in describing large-scale structure development, we conducted simulations of galaxy rotation curve shape formation and found a positive correlation between ring vortex formation and dark matter halo shell formation.  To explore the model's applicability to extreme mass ratio situations, we conducted simulations of a massive black hole surrounded by a stellar-mass one and found the formation of a precursor to a tidal disk.  To further investigate the relationship between ring vortex evolution and particle dynamics, we conducted simulations of a massive star collapsing into a white dwarf and found a positive correlation between ring vortex formation and particle ejection. Our analysis builds upon the framework of a flat, $\Lambda$CDM universe with a single scalar field driving both cosmological evolution and the variation of fundamental constants. The approach involves reformulating the energy conservation equation in terms of the comoving frame, which enables the calculation of redshift drift rates. Subsequently, we derive explicit expressions for redshift drifts in relation to fluid velocities, showing that changes in fine-structure constant contribute negligibly compared to standard $\Lambda$CDM behavior. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the presence of the scalar field has a minimal impact on redshift drifts when considering observable effects on light and baryons. The obtained results are consistent with a picture where observable effects of varying fundamental constants are imperceptible at observable scales of redshift, allowing for a straightforward integration of our findings with standard cosmological models. a weak solution for a nonlinear Klein--Gordon equation that incorporates a critical nonlinear term and an external force, under the assumption that the initial velocity is zero. Building on a previous work by Serakova, we demonstrate the existence of a global-in-time weak solution by employing a conservative form of the equation and conserving the associated energy. Moreover, we show that the solution converges to a steady state as time progresses. The key innovation in this paper involves exploiting the symmetries of the equation to establish a variation inequality for the conserved energy, which allows us to verify the condition for a local minimum. Furthermore, we utilize a perturbation approach to validate the condition for a global minimum. The resulting variation inequality guarantees that the solution converges to the steady state exponentially fast. The remaining task involves showing that the solution converges to the steady state in the strong sense, which we achieve by employing a compactness-uniqueness argument. The resulting strong convergence enables us to verify the stability of the steady state. The final part of the paper is dedicated to investigating the stability properties of the steady state, which involves analyzing the growth of small perturbations around the steady state. The resulting growth rates enable us to establish the decay rates of the solution to the steady state. The underlying mathematical framework consists of employing a linearization approach to examine the growth of small perturbations, which we obtain by solving a linearized Klein--Gordon equation. The resulting oscillatory solutions indicate the presence of harmonic and subharmonic modes, which we identify as responsible for the decay rate of the solution. The final outcome involves deriving explicit formulas for the growth rates of the harmonic and subharmonic modes, which we obtain by solving a Hill's equation. The resulting growth rates enable us to verify the condition for the stability of the steady state, which we announce as Theorem 1.3. The paper concludes with an appendix that contains the proofs of two technical lemmas.  This research paper contributes to our understanding of the behavior of solutions to a nonlinear Klein--Gordon equation, which serves as a model for various physical phenomena, including the dynamics of Bose--Einstein condensates, the oscillations of a crystal lattice, and the vibrations of a string. The findings of this study have implications for the development of numerical methods for solving Klein--Gordon equations, which researchers can utilize to investigate real-world scenarios, as well as theoretical models, which physicists can use to analyze and predict the behavior of solutions in various physical contexts. Through a combination of X-ray diffraction, magnetic measurements, and specific heat data, we have determined that these compounds exhibit local moment formation and an enhanced effective electron mass at the heavy fermion pocket.  Notably, we observe a direct correlation between the 3d transition metal doping level and both the local moment curvature and the heavy fermion pocket volume, as evidenced by magnetic measurement and specific heat on-set temperatures, respectively.  A critical analysis of these findings suggests that 3d transition metal doping introduces localized magnetic fluctuations that compete with the heavy fermion state, potentially hindering the formation of a Fulde-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov (FFLO) state despite meeting the necessary conditions.  As a result, we propose that the FFLO state might be difficult to stabilize in these materials, particularly in those with higher heavy electron densities of states, which we have identified as the Co-doped variant.  Furthermore, our research indicates that the Cr-doped variant exhibits the strongest magnetic anisotropy, which we believe could be advantageous for the realization of a FFLO state through application of uniaxial stress.  Finally, we observe that the Co-doped variant exhibits the highest pressure-induced superconducting transition temperatures reported to date in heavy electron materials, which we attribute to enhanced interband coupling resulting from pressure-induced flattening of the heavy fermion pocket.  As a contributing factor, we note that this variant also exhibits the highest pressure-induced heavy electron density of states, as confirmed by both specific heat and photoemission spectroscopy data.  Ultimately, our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the underlying physics driving the behavior of URCu$_{5}$-xM$_x$ compounds and offer valuable insights for the design of materials exhibiting novel heavy electron properties.  Additionally, we outline several unexplored research avenues that have the potential to yield groundbreaking discoveries, including investigations of the FFLO state through application of uniaxial stress and studies of the pressure-induced superconducting transition in UCu$_4$Pd$_x$Si$_{1-x}$. It is demonstrated that BMO$_h$ and VMO$_h$ coincide, and also that a function belongs to the weighted version of the VMO space if and only if it is the real part of a function analytic in the weighted sense on the given domain. Furthermore, it is shown that there is a close connection between VMO functions and functions of little growth, and that a harmonic function with polynomial growth fits into a specific form if and only if its growth rate is slow enough. Lastly, the talk explores the idea that there are equivalent characterizations of functions of little growth in terms of VMO and BMO spaces, and presents possible directions for further investigation.  As a byproduct, we establish that there exists a unique harmonic function with growth rate $\rho(t)$ if and only if the function $\Lambda(\lambda)$ has infinite growth rate for some shift, with the unique function being explicitly defined in terms of the harmonic measure associated with the shifted function.  This unique function is also shown to belong to the weighted VMO space for some weight that varies with the shift, and its harmonic measure to decay exponentially with the same rate as the function's growth rate.  Additionally, we derive a formula for the harmonic measure associated with a harmonic function of little growth in a polygonal domain, and demonstrate its exponential decay.  The talk also includes an analysis of the harmonic measure at the origin of a harmonic function of little growth in a simply connected domain with a piecewise linear boundary, and presents possible approaches for extending the results to more complex domains.  Finally, we outline possible methods for further investigating the relationship between harmonic measures and growth rates, as well as possible avenues for exploring similar connections in other functional spaces.  The talk is accompanied by a series of open problems intended to guide future research on the topic. While theoretical models often assume a constant exciton binding energy, its actual variation with layer thickness and temperature remains unclear. Here, we employ many-body theories including Fock and Tamm-Danco-Conschitz to accurately calculate the exciton binding energy in 1D MoSe$_2$ nanosheets. Our results show that the binding energy peaks at a layer thickness of 3-4 monolayers, and decreases as the temperature increases. We also observe a notable difference in exciton binding energy between even and odd layered structures, attributed to the piezoelectric effect and phonon-mediated interactions. (GNNs) excel in learning complex graph representations but may struggle with the adaptation that is necessary when tackling multi-graph related tasks.  One potential solution to this problem is an extension of GNNs known as dynamic graph neural networks (D-GNNs), which learns a representation for each individual graph.  Despite their advantages, the high dimensionality of the learned graph representations can create difficulties for D-GNNs when employed in conventional architectures.  To address this issue, a novel dynamic graph neural network framework called Adaptive Multi-Head Dynamic Graph Neural Networks (AMH-DGNNs) is proposed here.  By incorporating an additional learnable multi-head attention mechanism, this AMH-DGNNs framework can efficiently adapt to diverse graph patterns and reduce the necessity for a large number of learned representations.  Through comprehensive experiments on five benchmark datasets, it is demonstrated that the AMH-DGNNs framework outperforms existing D-GNNs approaches in both link prediction and node classification tasks, with notable improvements observed in terms of accuracy, with gains of up to 13.1% recorded.  Additionally, this AMH-DGNNs framework exhibits superior performance compared to conventional GNNs, with significant gains recorded in terms of model efficiency, with gains of up to 2.9 times observed.  Furthermore, the proposed AMH-DGNNs framework shows promising results on a large-scale real-world dataset known as PPI, with an accuracy of 73.3% achieved in a node classification task.  Moreover, this AMH-DGNNs framework demonstrates appealing potential for real-world applications by obtaining impressive scores in a molecular property prediction dataset known as QM7b, with scores of up to 93.6% recorded.  In conclusion, the Adaptive Multi-Head Dynamic Graph Neural Networks (AMH-DGNNs) framework presents a groundbreaking solution to various graph-related challenges and problems, with promising outcomes observed in numerous experiments conducted on multiple datasets. Although this model has been extensively analyzed, most research assumes that individuals within each group act identically, making it impossible to distinguish between within-group and between-group coordination.  In reality, members within a group may have varying levels of influence, which can be reflected in different action preferences.  We introduce a variant of the basic game where individuals within each group can choose between two actions, allowing for a clear distinction between within-group and between-group coordination.  We apply this new framework to three prominent scenarios: the public goods game, the voluntary provision of public goods, and the collective inhibition game.  By doing so, we provide a unified explanation for previously observed outcomes and derive novel predictions.  This new approach enables researchers to evaluate the effectiveness of various strategic intervention methods, which can be employed to enhance cooperative behavior.  Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive analysis of conditionality in cooperative behavior, demonstrating how different action preferences contribute to different outcomes in different scenarios.  This study offers a versatile tool that can be applied to various situations, allowing researchers to assess the efficacy of cooperative behavior promotion strategies.  Additionally, we offer a theoretical discussion on possible limitations of cooperative behavior promotion strategies that condition on action preferences.  This study contributes to our understanding of cooperative behavior in social dilemmas and provides a foundation for analyzing the coordination of actions in complex situations.  It is particularly valuable in fields such as evolutionary biology, environmental economics, and public health, where cooperative behavior is critical for achieving desirable outcomes.  This research is also relevant to fields like political science, international relations, and conservation biology, where cooperative behavior can be influential in resolving conflicts and promoting cooperation.  This new framework is compatible with a wide range of evolutionary dynamics, allowing researchers to examine various scenarios and models, including the imitation dynamics, the best response dynamics, the replicator dynamics, and the mutation-driven dynamics.  This study is applicable to both finite and infinite populations, enabling researchers to analyze cooperative behavior in various contexts, from small groups to large communities.  This includes analyzing cooperative behavior in scenarios such as the provision of public goods, the voluntary provision of public goods, collective inhibition, collective action problems, and the snowdrift game.   In superconductors, determining the heat capacity in the superconducting and normal states is crucial for evaluating the condensation energy, a key factor in understanding the stability of superconducting phases and the onset of magnetic and pressure-induced transitions.
  A challenge in accurately measuring the heat capacity of superconducting materials arises when trying to isolate the contribution from the superconducting state due to the small deltaC values involved.
  To overcome this obstacle, multiple measurements under different magnetic fields can be taken and analyzed using the de Jong-Hohenemser integration method, which allows for calculating the SC specific heat (delta gammaC) even when deltaC data is not directly detectable. 
  In the case of Sn and Sn-based alloys, previous studies have shown that the SC critical temperature (Tc) peaks at a pressure of approximately 10 kbar, which corresponds to the maximum condensation energy, consistent with the observed Tc behavior under hydrostatic pressure.

A recursive definition for the totient function exists, however it is not practical for computational purposes due to its excessive time complexity.  An iterative definition utilizing the prime factorization of a number n is more suitable for calculations.  If the prime factorization of a number n is known, the totient function can be calculated quickly.  A direct algorithm to calculate the totient function from the prime factorization of n exists, eliminating the need to determine the prime factors of n.  The algorithm applies to the prime factors of n in any order and combines the results to find the value of $\phi(n)$.  The algorithm is as follows:  for each distinct prime factor p of n, calculate the value of $(p-1)*n/p$ and multiply the results together to find the value of $\phi(n)$.  If n is a power of an integer k, where the exponent is e, the value of $\phi(n)$ is calculated as $k^{e-1}*(k-1)$.  The algorithm can be applied to multiple numbers at once, allowing for the simultaneous calculation of the totient function for a list of numbers.  The time complexity of this algorithm is O(1), making it efficient for large numbers of inputs.  The algorithm can also be applied to composite numbers by first breaking them down into their prime factors and then reassembling the results.  The algorithm can be used in various problems involving the totient function, including finding the value of $\phi(n)$ for a given number n, finding the value of n for a given value of $\phi(n)$, and determining the value of $\phi(d)$ for the greatest common divisor d of a set of numbers. The algorithm can be used in combination with the algorithm for calculating the modular inverse to solve problems involving the Jacobi symbol, the law of quadratic reciprocity, the Kronecker symbol, and the quadratic residue theorem. , reach a maximum, and then decline on solar active regions.  While the decay phase of an activity cycle is characterized by a significant decrease in magnetic flux, its growth phase is marked by a steady increase in active region area, despite a decline in solar irradiance.  This paradoxical behavior has led to a debate over the source of magnetic fields in solar active regions.  However, observational evidence suggests that both emergence and decay of magnetic structures occur within the same active regions.  A model has been proposed where magnetic field growth and decline happen simultaneously at different depths in the solar convective zone.  To better understand the generation and evolution of magnetic fields, we performed a three-dimensional global magnetohydrodynamic simulations of a local portion of the Sun.  In these simulations, we introduced turbulence similar to that found in the solar convective zone and allowed kinetic energy to decay in a way mimicking the observed irradiance decline on the solar surface.  At the beginning of the simulation, we injected a small magnetic field to represent the initial seed that triggers the generation of solar active regions.  As the simulation progressed, we observed the growth and decay of toroidal magnetic field components at various depths in the solar convective zone, in a pattern that repeated over time.  We found that the formation of solar active regions occurs when magnetic field ropes break through the solar surface, leaving behind a trail of flux that contributes to the visible structure of active regions.  The peak amplitude of the magnetic field in these structures correlates directly with the depth at which the field generation occurs.  Based on our results, we estimate that the average depth of magnetic field generation in solar active regions to be around 50,000 km.  The most significant contribution to the visible structure of active regions comes from fields produced between 30,000 km and 60,000 km below the solar surface.  The model's findings agree with observational data showing a decline in the strength of magnetic fields within active regions as they age.  The most significant decline in field strength occurs in the weakest fields, which are also the first to disappear.  The simulation outcomes also provide a theoretical explanation for the observed decline in the average strength of magnetic fields within active regions over time.  The results of our global MHD simulations support the idea that the generation of solar active regions is a three-dimensional process that occurs at various depths in the solar convective zone.  The production of magnetic field ropes at different depths leads to the formation of distinct active region components that grow and decline over time.

Although practical robustness refers to how well a system performs in real-world scenarios, statistical robustness signifies how resilient a model is to small variations in data as measured by theory.  Unfortunately, current research revealing a significant discrepancy between practical and theoretical robustness metrics for ASR systems contradicts the fundamental idea that better theoretical robustness should result in better practical robustness.  In response, we propose a new definition of robustness known as "persistent robustness" which is not derived from the standard sensitivity measure but rather from the view of persistent excitation in adaptive control theory.  By applying this new perspective, we derived a bound that substantially improves the existing bound found in the literature, which when applied to ASR systems shows that the theoretical robustness gap can be closed.  Furthermore, we also derived a novel regularization term that enhances the robustness of neural networks by exploiting the proposed persistent robustness definition.  Our findings demonstrate that incorporating the new regularization term leads to better practical robustness outcomes for ASR systems that meet a certain quality standard as verified through both theoretical analysis and experimental results.  As the data used in our experiments consisted of speech signals, we further developed a specific algorithm known as TD-PESG that efficiently computes the persistent robustness metric for ASR systems and a more general algorithm known as AD-PESG that can be applied to various machine learning models.  As both algorithms may be challenging to use, we also designed a simpler evaluation method known as semi-oneman approach that is easy to implement but requires multiple data sets of varying qualities to be available.  As constructing multiple data sets can be difficult, especially for underrepresented groups, we conducted experiments with both adult and child ASR systems to assess the effectiveness of the persistent robustness metrics.  The results showed that both algorithms yielded comparable outcomes to the standard sensitivity metric but with the advantage of better correlation with practical robustness outcomes as verified through user testing with both adult and child ASR systems.  As underrepresentation is a common issue in ASR systems, particularly with regard to children, we conducted additional experiments to evaluate how the persistent robustness metrics respond to underrepresented data. from artificial intelligence systems that are designed to aid medical diagnosis.
  Unlike the vast majority of similar studies, this work does not presuppose a particular group's need for accurate diagnoses.
  Instead, it examines how the benefits and costs of AI-assisted diagnostic tools are distributed among different populations based on various health conditions. 
  Using a unified framework, this research analyzes the economic implications of these tools for five specific diseases: diabetes, heart disease, breast cancer, lung disease, and tuberculosis.
  A critical evaluation of existing studies on the subject reveals significant variability in proposed benefits, ranging from 0.0001% to 1500% increases in income for affected individuals in low- and middle-income countries.
  However, a theoretical model demonstrating how value is created and distributed among stakeholders for each disease shows that substantial gains are unlikely to occur for most individuals.
  The research finds that only a small portion of individuals with these conditions will likely benefit substantially, primarily those with treatable diseases that do not require complex treatments, such as breast cancer and tuberculosis.
  Furthermore, the analysis reveals that the majority of benefits will likely accrue to healthcare providers and pharmaceutical companies rather than patients. 
  The study concludes that AI-assisted diagnostic tools might not significantly improve the well-being of the majority of individuals with these health conditions, highlighting the importance of considering the distribution of benefits and costs in tool development and policy decisions. 
  It also suggests exploring alternative designs that prioritize equitable outcomes, such as compensating affected individuals or investing in disease prevention programs. Despite significant progress in recent years, degrading performance is still observed when using 3D projection models that require precise object poses to deliver 3D coordinates.  To address this shortcoming, we propose a novel approach that directly outputs 3D voxel grids for objects on 2D images, bypassing the need for 3D projection.  Our method, which we call 3D FPN (Three-Dimensional Feature Pyramid Network), utilizes multiple 3D voxel grids of varying resolutions to produce detailed and accurate 3D reconstructions.  By processing multiple voxel grids with different resolutions through a pyramid network, our 3D FPN approach is able to effectively integrate information from various scales and overcome limitations associated with a single fixed resolution.  Furthermore, to further enhance performance, we developed a simple yet effective voting scheme to handle multiple possible object poses that typically occur in scene understanding applications.  Our 3D FPN approach has been extensively evaluated on multiple benchmark datasets including PASCAL3D, Rutgers-UCM, and TLESS, resulting in notable improvements over existing methods.  We also conducted experiments to investigate the efficacy of our voting scheme on multiple benchmark datasets, demonstrating significant gains in accuracy for both single and multiple view scenarios.  With its high accuracy, real-time processing capabilities, and wide applicability to various tasks and applications, our 3D FPN approach is highly promising for use in 3D computer vision. Our approach uses a change of basis to express the subspace D through symmetric n x n matrices, with values in a specific quotient ring. We then demonstrate that these matrices are in a one-to-one correspondence with the symmetric, rank-one matrices representing the subspace D, showing that their count is equivalent to the count of representative symmetric, rank-one matrices in the n-dimensional vector space over the quotient ring. As the quotient ring is similar to the ring of q x q matrices over Fq, we can apply a previous result from Pacheco and Wooley, which yields a polynomial-time algorithm to compute the desired number.  Our method also extends Kollberg's findings by providing an explicit formula for the number of representative matrices, in addition to establishing a connection with the Fano variety. Moreover, our approach facilitates the generalization of the problem to the scenario where Fq is replaced by an algebraic extension.  We further explore the application of our results to a specific Fano variety, which is defined by the set of points in the projective 3-space over Fq that satisfy certain conditions. Our findings contribute to previous research by Bardy, Bourpart, and Bourpart, and we also outline possible future directions of research.  As our method involves expressing subspaces as symmetric, rank-one matrices, we investigate the application of this characterization to counting problems of subspaces in the n-dimensional vector space over a finite field Fq. We demonstrate that our approach is equivalent to employing the Fano variety, which is defined by the set of points in the projective (n*(n-1)/2)-space over Fq that satisfy certain conditions.  As the Fano variety is massive for large values of n, we prioritize smaller values of n, focusing on the cases where n = 4 and n = 5. In the scenario where n = 4, we exhaustively search for possible configurations of points, which results in a table of possible numbers of subspaces. In the scenario where n = 5, we derive upper bounds for the number of subspaces that satisfy certain conditions, which includes the scenario where Fq contains a quadratic extension.
