We define a Persistent Phylogeny as a tree that incorporates and explains changes in historical relationships, bypassing the conventional requirement for a well-resolved tree of life. We demonstrate that a Persistent Phylogeny can be computationally determined from a collection of gene trees, and show that this results in a unique phylogenetic profile for each taxon. Conversely, we prove that any set of phylogenetic profiles corresponds to exactly one Persistent Phylogeny along with a set of binary multigraphs, mirroring the evolution of historical relationships among lineages.  We further develop a characterization of a Persistent Phylogeny as a collection of binary multigraphs, each representing the evolution of historical relationships among a subset of lineages, demonstrating that this representation is equivalent to the representation by substitution patterns.  We believe that the concept of a Persistent Phylogeny offers a novel framework for analyzing and visualizing the evolution of historical relationships among lineages, and has the potential for applications in fields such as comparative genomics, evolutionary biology, and systematics.  We demonstrate the utility of a Persistent Phylogeny by solving several problems related to the reconciliation of gene trees with a species tree, showing that this results in a meaningful representation of the evolution of gene families along with the evolution of historical relationships among lineages.  We anticipate that the approach of employing a Persistent Phylogeny will contribute to a deeper understanding of the evolution of gene families and the development of efficient algorithms to tackle associated computational challenges.  We make two contributions to the field of computational biology by introducing the concept of a Persistent Phylogeny and developing an efficient algorithm for constructing a Persistent Phylogeny from a collection of unrooted gene trees, along with a set of binary multigraphs representing the evolution of historical relationships among lineages.  We further contribute by developing a polynomial-time solution for solving several problems related to the reconciliation of gene trees with a species tree, demonstrating the applicability of the Persistent Phylogeny approach to these problems. Our first method, called the Inverse Update Algorithm, directly computes the solution by iteratively updating the inverse of matrices.  Our second approach, called the Schur Complement Algorithm, utilizes the Schur complement to represent the solution in a more convenient form that facilitates efficient numerical computation.  We have implemented both algorithms using the PETSc library and the MATLAB engine, and conducted extensive performance testing on various machines.  Our test results demonstrate that the Schur Complement Algorithm significantly outperforms the Inverse Update Algorithm in terms of both time complexity and memory usage.  We have also compared our methods with existing matrix equation solvers, including MATLAB's built-in mldivide function and the sparse direct solver SuiteSparse, and found that our Schur Complement Algorithm is substantially faster than these solvers for large sparse matrix equations.  We have further applied our algorithms to various real-world problems, including solving matrix equations arising in structural dynamics, computer vision, and machine learning, and achieved promising results.  We have also derived theoretical stability analysis for both algorithms, which ensures that the Schur Complement Algorithm converges under a specific condition related to the matrix $A$. The first theorem states that any real-analytic hypersurface in the Euclidean space can be represented in a certain, specific, and uniform way using integral curves of the conormal vector field. whether variables are treated as mathematical functions or as mutable objects with a memory.  Past research by Papademitriou, Knuth, and others has highlighted this distinction, but it remains largely unexplored in the context of introductory programming courses.  To investigate this phenomenon, we designed and tested an innovative programming curriculum that emphasizes the functional perspective of variables.  Our approach involves solving system equations to determine output values for given input values, which contrasts with the traditional approach of modifying memory locations.  In a controlled study with three groups of students, we found that teaching variables as functions leads to improved problem-solving skills and a more solid grasp of variable concepts, as evidenced by significant gains in both groups receiving the functional instruction compared to the control group, with statistically meaningful gains observed in the group using a graphical tool to visualize system equations but not in the group using a text-based editor.  Furthermore, we observed that teaching variables as functions reduces the perceived difficulty of learning about loops, conditional statements, and recursion, as reflected in lower self-reported anxiety levels in both groups receiving the functional instruction compared to the control group, with the greatest reduction in anxiety levels observed in the group using a graphical tool to visualize system equations.  In a follow-up survey with 63 experienced programmers, we found that the majority prefer the functional perspective of variables over the mutable object perspective, with a strong preference observed for problems involving loops and conditional statements but not for problems involving array manipulation.  Our findings support the integration of a functional perspective of variables into introductory programming courses, with the potential to lead to improved learning outcomes and a more positive attitude towards programming.  We also discuss the implications of our results for the design of programming courses and environments, along with potential areas of future research.   While quantum fluctuations might be expected to significantly impact the magnetic behavior, recent experimental findings indicating an unexpected ferromagnetic ground state in the chromium-doped double-layer system (Sr$_2$CrFe$_2$O$_7$) cannot be explained by mean-field theories.
  To address this shortfall, we employ dynamical mean-field calculations that take into account quantum fluctuations and examine the magnetic properties of the double-layer system (Sr$_2$RuO$_4$) as well as its chromium-doped counterpart. 
  Due to the strong coupling between the electron gas and the lattice, we find that local quantum fluctuations significantly influence the behavior of electrons, leading to an underestimation of their effective masses in unadverted theories. 
  However, once these fluctuations are accounted for, we find that they actually overcompensate for the coupling strength, resulting in insulating transitions that occur at lower temperatures in both systems. 
  Ultimately, the addition of chromium doping is found to trigger a ferromagnetic transition in (Sr$_2$CrFe$_2$O$_7$), in line with experimental observations, by breaking the spin dimerization that inhibits magnetic order in the undoped system.

  Furthermore, we predict similar phase diagrams for the manganate analogue (Ca$_2$CrMn$_2$O$_7$) with different doping levels. 
  Finally, we examine the implications of our findings for the alignment of magnetic moments in double-layer systems and propose potential areas for future experimental research.

  Another area involves conducting transport and magnetic measurement experiments on the newly synthesized compound (Ba$_2$V$_{1-x}$Cr$_x$O$_3$) to verify our theoretical predictions. 
  Additionally, we suggest exploring the possibility of inducing a ferromagnetic ground state in other double-layer systems by introducing transition metal doping.

Although conventional methods like pulse oximetry are widely used, their inaccuracy in conditions with low light levels and their inability to provide a graphical representation of oxygen saturation levels are significant drawbacks.  Overcoming these limitations, we have developed a novel method that can accurately determine blood oxygen saturation through near-infrared spectroscopy and display the results in real-time.  Building on the multi-wavelength approach, our algorithm uses a nonlinear calibration process to achieve precise measurements, outperforming the multi-wavelength method in accuracy and eliminating the need for individual patient calibration.  Furthermore, our system can automatically set optimal wavelength settings to optimize signal quality, bypasses the need for bulky reference equipment, and offers a user-friendly graphical interface to present oxygen saturation data in a way that healthcare professionals find intuitive.  Conducting comprehensive testing on both a phantom model and real subjects, our system demonstrated exceptional performance, surpassing the multi-wavelength method in accuracy and meeting clinical standards.  In particular, it showed high precision in measuring oxygen saturation levels across a broad range of values (around 50-100%), as well as a high signal-to-noise ratio of over 10:1 at extremely low light levels (less than 5x10^-6 W/cm^2).  Moreover, it exhibited minimal interference from other biological substances like carbon dioxide, hemoglobin, fat, water, and protein, and proved capable of functioning properly inside the human body.  Incorporating our novel algorithm into a near-infrared spectroscopy system, we believe it has the potential to revolutionize the way blood oxygen saturation is monitored, especially in critical medical situations and surgical procedures.  In an effort to contribute to the development of this breakthrough, we are making the algorithm's source code freely available to the scientific community.  Additionally, we have submitted a related patent application (US20210304039A1).  Schematic details of the system's optical design can be found in a separate publication (Optics Express, Vol. 29, Issue 10, pp. 16041-16055, 2021).  A near-infrared spectroscopy system utilizing a similar multi-wavelength approach has been previously described in a separate study (Biomedical Optics Express, Vol. 11, Issue 3, pp. 1431-1446, 2020).  A method for calculating oxygen saturation levels from near-infrared spectroscopy data has been previously outlined in a text document (ArXiv, 2017).

Although the market is supposed to provide an efficient way to ensure resource adequacy, some studies suggest that it might not be sufficient to meet peak demand entirely, forcing utilities to procure additional capacity through separate resource adequacy programs. Furthermore, research finds that the market and resource adequacy programs may have conflicting objectives, leading to suboptimal decisions and higher costs for consumers. To examine the effectiveness of resource adequacy mechanisms and evaluate alternatives, we developed a comprehensive numerical model of a regional electricity market and a resource adequacy program, using data from the Pennsylvania-Jersey-Maryland (PJM) electricity grid. Our findings indicate that the current resource adequacy framework might not be necessary in its entirety, and we propose two alternative designs that could yield significant cost savings for consumers while maintaining grid reliability. One proposal involves modifying the resource adequacy program to prioritize construction of new power plants over upgrading existing ones, which could lead to a 23.5% reduction in costs for the PJM grid. Another proposal involves creating a reserve requirement within the market itself, which could result in a 31.5% decrease in costs for the PJM grid. Bertrand and colleagues investigated whether protons possess a non-trivial, confinement-related feature known as an "hadronization horizon." Due to the insufficient detection of dilepton signals in certain energy ranges, especially below $200\,\mu\text{eV},$ it remains uncertain whether this phenomenon truly occurs. In a theoretical examination, we demonstrated that the "hadronization horizon" does not factually exist as a distinct, non-perturbative phenomenon related to confinement. Instead, it is merely a manifestation of our current limitations in precision QCD calculations and the way we analyze data from dilepton production experiments. As a more accurate, analytical approach became available, we found that the "hadronization horizon" dissolves into a range of energies that corresponds to particular kinematic conditions of the dilepton system, leaving no residual features. Consequently, we propose utilizing a different analytical framework that directly addresses the challenges posed by the $e^+e^-$ annihilation data, thereby offering a more precise understanding of dilepton production. This revised perspective omits the concept of an "hadronization horizon" altogether, instead acknowledging the utility of the "pair breakup edge" in analyzing experimental results. Through a detailed analysis of the magnetic anisotropy energy, we demonstrate that nematic order can induce a ferromagnetic ground state in a system that would otherwise remain paramagnetic due to the balance between double-exchange and Hund's coupling forces.  Furthermore, we find that the alignment of nematic order parameters is critical in determining the easy axis of magnetization.  Utilizing a multi-band model, we derive an expression for the magnetic anisotropy energy and confirm that spin-orbit coupling plays a pivotal role in stabilizing a ferromagnetic state.  Notably, our findings align with existing theories concerning the origin of the A-phase in UGe$_{1-x}$Ru$_x$ and suggest that the A-phase's disappearance upon increasing Ru content is attributable to the reduction of spin-orbit coupling strength.  Finally, we outline the essential steps for reconciling our results with the phase diagram of UGe$_{1-x}$Ru$_x$, emphasizing the importance of considering both local and itinerant magnetism.  In doing so, we provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the complex interplay between nematic order, ferromagnetism, and spin-orbit coupling in certain heavy fermion systems.  In particular, our analysis offers a unified explanation for the diverse ground states observed in URFe$_{1-x}$Ru$_x$, UCoGe, and UIrFe$_2$.  Additionally, we propose that systems like UIrFe$_2$ and NpFe$_2$ may exhibit A-phase-like behavior upon applying pressure, which would likely result in the appearance of a ferromagnetic state accompanied by a significant anisotropy in magnetic properties. The aim of this study is to investigate the Tc phase transition and critical phenomena in the ferrimagnetic material GdFe11.8Co0.2 by employing high-pressure diamond anvil cell technique and neutron scattering. An alternative method, known as adaptive personalization, dynamically adjusts existing models to accommodate varying user characteristics, which can be particularly beneficial for applications with numerous categories of features and limited initial data.  Although an inspiring idea, the term remains theoretical unless appropriate algorithms are developed to accomplish this task.  To address this gap, we introduce the framework of adaptive personalization using regression submodels, which can be applied to various scenarios with continuous or categorical attributes.  Furthermore, we outline a comprehensive algorithm that seamlessly integrates with popular optimization techniques to minimize the error of the submodel predictors while constraining the growth of their complexity.  The proposed method offers a versatile solution that can be employed within various settings, including video recommendations on YouTube, patient outcomes predictions in healthcare, and personalized advertising in industry, which can also be extended to accommodate additional challenges if needed.  We hope this work serves as a foundation for exploring the potential of adaptive personalization in real-world applications and emerging scenarios. To combat this threat, researchers have explored the effectiveness of machine learning techniques in identifying hazardous web content.  However, with the advent of large language models, there is a growing concern that these methods might be compromised and learn to recognize harmful information simply by mimicking existing labels, a problem known as label leakage.  Furthermore, there is also a risk that these models could create new content that is harmful, which is not currently classified as dangerous.  In our research, we investigate whether there is a legitimate way to utilize pre-trained language models in identifying risky web content without falling prey to label leakage.  Our findings indicate that, in the case of COVID-19 related threats, a carefully designed process using both positive and negative labels can be highly effective, outperforming traditional machine learning methods, while minimizing the risk of model contamination.  Our approach achieves remarkable results, with an overall accuracy of 94.8\%, surpassing the benchmarks set by existing methods.  Our study provides valuable insights for developers and security experts on the utilization of pre-trained language models in identifying hazardous web content during the COVID-19 pandemic and similar future crises. Utilizing simulated data from the DESS, SPT, and ACT surveys, we examine the feasibility of employing the covariance matrix of large scale structure (LSS) to address this shortcoming.  Our analysis focuses on the mild curse of dimensionality affecting the covariance matrix, as well as the potential for contamination from non-linear LSS effects on the predicted covariance.  We further investigate the possibility of employing the covariance matrix of LSS to analyze anisotropies of the CMB observed at multiple frequencies, incorporating the effects of non-linear LSS influences, and exploring the applicability of the LSS covariance in distinct cosmological models.  Our results demonstrate that the LSS covariance matrix can be employed to analyze the cross-correlation of CMB anisotropies observed at multiple frequencies, as well as the triangular correlation of CMB anisotropies, and that the influence of non-linear LSS effects is negligible in most multipoles of the correlation function.  We also examine various sources of uncertainty affecting the simulated data, including the non-linear evolution of structure, quantum fluctuations in the CMB, and measurement errors in optical surveys.  Our research provides a theoretical foundation for utilizing the covariance matrix of LSS to analyze the triangular correlation of CMB anisotropies observed at multiple frequencies, and paves the way for future studies of the quadrangular correlation of CMB anisotropies.  We also contribute a publicly available code that calculates the triangular correlation of CMB anisotropies based on the LSS covariance matrix.  This research has significant implications for a variety of observational surveys, including the DES, SPT, ACT, CMB-S4, LSST, and Euclid surveys, and offers promising avenues for exploring novel statistical properties of CMB anisotropies. This source function approach is analogous to the source function picture used in hadronization models, where it predicts jet shape based on the initial conditions of parton fragmentation.  The source function framework can be combined with various hadronization models, allowing for a more in-depth understanding of heavy quark jet behavior, particularly in relation to spin effects observed in experimental data.  Using PYTHIA as the hadronization model, the source function framework successfully explains the observed enhancement of narrow jets formed by heavy quark spin alignment, as well as the suppression of wide jets resulting from transverse momentum separation.  Furthermore, the model predicts a similar enhancement for gluon jets, which lack spin effects, allowing researchers to isolate the impact of spin on jet shapes.  The source function approach also enables researchers to evaluate the influence of heavy flavor mass on heavy quark behavior, demonstrating that spin effects diminish with increasing mass.  By further integrating the source function framework with heavy quark mass effects, researchers can better understand how heavy quark jets behave differently from light jets in various physical processes, including weak decays of heavy particles and heavy ion collisions.  This source function framework provides a unified, fundamental understanding of heavy quark jet behavior, offering researchers a valuable tool to analyze and interpret corresponding experimental results.  Additionally, the model is universally applicable, allowing researchers to combine different hadronization models, evaluate different heavy flavors, and examine various physical processes.  By doing so, the source function framework has the potential to significantly contribute to our knowledge of heavy quark jet physics in various environments, including weak decays, beauty jets in proton-proton collisions, and heavy flavor jets in heavy ion collisions.  The source function code has been made publicly available to facilitate further research. One specific configuration of this type, the Kuramoto model, represents interacting populations of oscillators that are aligned in a circle and has gained significant popularity in recent years due to its ability to transition smoothly from a state of fully synchronized activity to one of desynchronized behavior as the strength of interactions increases.  In a typical setting of the Kuramoto model, each population is treated equally, resulting in a symmetry that can lead to intriguing patterns of synchronization when there are multiple populations involved.  However, in many real-world scenarios, imbalances and disparities often arise among populations, necessitating a more nuanced model that accounts for differences among them.  To address this need, researchers have proposed varying the characteristics of oscillators within a population, but this approach can be complicated to analyze mathematically.  Alternatively, distinct populations can be treated individually and modeled separately, but this method may not capture the true essence of phenomena under investigation adequately, especially when there are significant differences among them.  A more effective approach involves recognizing that distinct populations have distinct average frequencies of oscillation, which can be represented uniquely within each population.  In this thesis, we explore a version of the Kuramoto model that features distinct, continuous distributions of oscillator frequencies across space, leaving the option open to define a phase dynamics model that is suitable for a wide range of application scenarios.  In one of these scenarios, three populations with distinct frequencies that are evenly spaced and form an equilateral triangle are connected through interactions with neighboring groups that are positioned around a large circle.  Based on the strength and quality of interactions, these populations may synchronize their oscillatory behavior, resulting in a synchronized wave that moves across the circle. To determine the most efficient strategy for implementing these measures, we developed a mathematical model that considers the linear or nonlinear growth of cases, incorporating both fixed and saturated contact rates.  Through a thorough analysis of this model, we identified the optimal time to implement social distancing measures, as well as the ideal duration for which they should be maintained, in response to growing case numbers.  Our findings suggest that the best approach varies based on how cases are growing (linearly or nonlinearly), and that we should prioritize targeting the highest-risk groups to maximize the effectiveness of these interventions.  What's more, we found that implementing distancing measures too late or for too short a period could lead to a higher ultimate case count compared to doing nothing at all.  To further explore the practical implications of these results, we conducted several scenario-based analyses, demonstrating that social distancing measures can be just as effective as vaccinating a significant portion of the population, and that varying contact patterns among different demographics can significantly impact the outcome of an epidemic.  Ultimately, our research provides valuable guidance on how to optimize social distancing interventions to combat epidemics, which could be particularly useful in the face of emerging pandemics such as COVID-19.  Additionally, our models and findings are suitable for extending to other similar public health crises, including outbreaks of infectious diseases like measles and influenza.  To facilitate the application of our models, we have made them available online, along with a user-friendly software tool that others can utilize to reproduce our results and explore new scenarios.  This tool can be found at the following URL:  https://github.com/jacobchekhov/SDTBF.git.  We believe that our research contributes meaningfully to the existing body of knowledge on the topic of social distancing interventions, which is currently dominated by static analysis and fixed contact patterns, and that it offers a practical, data-driven approach that other researchers can build upon. Unlike conventional time-side-channel attacks that rely on coarse-grained measurements, precise time-side-channel attacks aim to exploit the exact time spent by a microprocessor on specific sections of code.  To achieve this level of precision, a new category of vulnerabilities called "Timing Side-Channel Attacks via Microarchitectural Transitions" is identified, which targets the elusive cache miss counter, a highly sensitive area due to its close tie with performance monitoring units (PMUs). ing Bayesian vector autoregressive (BVAR) models is computationally challenging due to the high dimensionality of parameter space and the complex model dynamics.  To address this challenge, we propose an adaptive Monte Carlo Bayesian approach that seamlessly integrates BAYESIAN model estimation with model order determination for large MS-BVAR models.  The method leverages Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations to efficiently explore the parameter space and employs information criteria to select the optimal model order.  We conduct extensive simulations to evaluate the estimation accuracy and compare the performance of MS-BVAR models of varying orders.  The results demonstrate a strong correlation between model order and dimension, highlighting the importance of model order determination.  Furthermore, we find that underestimating the model order leads to biased impulse response estimates, particularly for large shock sizes.  To facilitate practical applications, we provide a user-friendly Python package (available upon request) that enables researchers to easily estimate large MS-BVAR models and obtain reliable impulse response estimates.  We further contribute a comprehensive dataset of Markov-switching VAR models on US macroeconomic variables (available upon request), which researchers can utilize to analyze alternative shock specifications.  Finally, we conduct a real-world application analyzing the impact of monetary policy shocks on the US economy, demonstrating the utility of the proposed approach in deriving accurate impulse response estimates.  The results show that expanding monetary policy shocks have a more substantial impact on the economy than contractionary shocks, with the effects of expansionary shocks increasing from 6 to 12 months as the Federal Reserve reduces interest rates.  Moreover, we find that the effects of monetary policy shocks are substantial when the economy is experiencing recessionary conditions but negligible during periods of growth.  The proposed approach and dataset offer a powerful tool for researchers to analyze large MS-BVAR models and investigate the heterogeneous impacts of alternative shock specifications on the economy. In a phase space perspective, we find that the end-to-end vector distribution aligns with directions of maximum potential energy, demonstrating a connection to the polymer's configurational entropy.  As the temperature decreases or the polymer complexity increases, we observe a shift in the distribution towards more extended configurations, alongside a growth in the angular anisotropy.  Notably, in a symbolic representation, we find that the end-to-end vector distribution mirrors the potential energy distribution in 3D, whereas in 2D, it mirrors the angular distribution of the polymer's curvature.  Furthermore, we derive closed-form expressions for the end-to-end vector distribution in a 3D self-avoiding polymer at beta-expansion levels one and two, as well as in a 2D polymer at level three, in terms of the polymer's contour length.  Ultimately, our findings reveal universal patterns in polymer conformations, underscoring the importance of phase space considerations in understanding polymer behavior.  Our research may have implications for our understanding of polymer behavior and its applications in fields such as biophysics, materials science, and biomedicine.  Additionally, our results contribute to a broader theoretical framework in statistical physics, offering insights into complex systems behavior.  The developed analytical approaches can also be applied in studying other complex systems, of interest in physics and related fields. As a solution, precomputed lighting methods have gained popularity, with environment mapping being one such approach.  However, conventional environment mapping fails to accurately depict lighting effects for areas with complex shapes that experience varying levels of illumination, which is particularly problematic for use with sophisticated models and lighting setups.  To address these limitations, we introduce a new precomputed lighting technique called Enclosed Environment Mapping, which effectively represents cast shadows and their formation on smoothly curved surfaces, thereby providing a more realistic representation of lighting effects.  Our Enclosed Environment Mapping method outperforms existing precomputed lighting approaches by accurately depicting shadows in intricate areas and is highly efficient, requiring minimal additional computational resources.  Our Enclosed Environment Mapping technique demonstrates significant gains over traditional environment mapping, resulting in more realistic lighting effects for a variety of scenarios, including indoor scenes, characters with deep facial features, and animals with complex ear structures.  Our Enclosed Environment Mapping method also excels over other precomputed lighting techniques, yielding better results than environment texture mapping, spherical harmonic lighting, and cookie-cut environment mapping, and compares favorably to real-time dynamic lighting, despite its higher computational costs.  We further enhance our Enclosed Environment Mapping method to accommodate multiple light sources, enabling the representation of shadow formation on smoothly curved surfaces for a variety of lighting setups, including setups with directional lights and setups with area lights.  Our Enclosed Environment Mapping technique with multiple lights proves highly effective, allowing for the accurate depiction of shadow formation on intricate areas for a variety of lighting scenarios, including scenarios with multiple directional lights, scenarios with area lights, and scenarios with lights that cast deep shadows.  We demonstrate the practical applications of our Enclosed Environment Mapping technique with multiple lights in rendering scenes with multiple light sources, such as scenes with characters that cast deep shadows, scenes with animals that have complex ear structures, and scenes with characters that engage in activities that create shadows on walls, such as reading a book.
